newsitem.title: USA: U.S. researchers see breakthrough with cloned calf.
newsitem.headline: U.S. researchers see breakthrough with cloned calf.

text.p: Gene, a cloned American calf, was introduced to the world on Thursday and researchers predicted the breakthrough proocess that created Gene had production line possibilities.

"We can make an unlimited number of cells, freeze them for any amount of time, then thaw them and make identical animals possessing a desired trait," said Michael Bishop, vice president of research at the company that created the cloned calf.
"Cells from cattle containing unique, favourable traits can be stored indefinitely, essentially preserving them for the future," he added.
The latest advance in a field that has expanded rapidly since researchers in Scotland created Dolly the sheep, the world's first cloned mammal, was announced by ABS Global Inc.

The company, a leading provider of bull semen and bovine reproductive services, said it had formed a subsidiary, Infigen, Inc., to commercialize applications of the technology in the cattle breeding, pharmaceutical, and other fields.

It said the process represents a "scientific breakthrough" that advances the prospects for commercializing cattle-cloning. It will offer an unlimited source of genetic material to cost effectively produce large numbers of cloned cattle in a more efficient way than other processes previously announced, it added.
The process begins with stem cells -- cells that determine genetic makeup -- which are taken from the foetus of a calf 30 days after conception.
The stem cells are treated with proteins that speed their growth and make them permanent stem cells that can be preserved indefinitely and will yield genetic duplicates of the original animal.

One of these cloned embryonic cells is then placed in an unfertilised cow's egg from which the nucleus was removed. A low voltage electric current is passed through the egg to fuse the new cell inside it.
The egg is placed in a growth media to make it divide several times. Eventually the embryo is placed inside a cow for a normal gestation period of 280 days.
Bishop said the technique can also be used to produce transgenic animals -- those that could carry human genes to produce therapeutic or pharmaceutical agents for treating human conditions.
The scientists in Scotland who produced Dolly introduced five cloned lambs with such human genes.
Marc van't Noordende, chief executive officer of ABS, said cloning and related technologies also promised to enhance "the quality, consistency and nutritional value of dairy and beef products ..."
It is considered slightly easier to use embryonic cells to make clones as they still have the natural potential to grow into complete animals.
In March, Australian scientists reported the cloning of 400 cattle using a technology that also begins with embryonic cells.
